cues.text: A Widow's Devotion in Saxon Norfolk
In the year 1061, during the reign of the pious King St. Edward the Confessor , a Saxon noblewoman named Richeldis de Faverches held the manor of Walsingham Parva in Norfolk.
Widowed young, Richeldis still had a son named Geoffrey to raise.

Even among her household, she was known for quiet prayer and generous charity toward the poor who came to her door—the ordinary, unremarkable holiness of a woman with no reason to expect Heaven would ever single her out.
We recognize in this ordinary beginning a pattern the Church has seen many times since.
Heaven so often chooses, for its most enduring works, not the powerful or the famous, but a widow praying quietly in an obscure corner of the world.
Taken in Spirit to Nazareth
According to a tradition recorded in a fifteenth-century ballad printed by Richard Pynson, Richeldis had prayed earnestly to know how she might honor the Mother of God.
She received her answer in a vision: Our Lady took her, in spirit, to the humble house at Nazareth where the Angel Gabriel had once announced Christ’s coming.
Our Lady asked her to build an exact replica of it at Walsingham, in devotion to the mystery of the Annunciation.
The tradition holds that this vision was repeated three times before Richeldis set herself to the task.
A House Completed in the Night
Richeldis had timber and materials prepared, but the builders, tradition tells us, struggled to raise the house on the site she had first chosen.
She spent a night in earnest prayer, and by morning the little house stood finished — moved, the faithful came to believe, by Our Lady's own hand.
It stood on a second dry patch of ground nearby, beside which a spring later rose.
Pilgrims would seek its waters for healing for centuries afterward.
England's Nazareth
News of the Holy House spread quickly, and within a few generations Walsingham became one of medieval Christendom's great pilgrimage shrines.
Kings, nobles, and ordinary pilgrims visited alike, so the village came to be called simply, "England's Nazareth."
Richeldis's own son Geoffrey provided canons to guard and serve the shrine.
By the mid-twelfth century, an Augustinian priory had grown around the little house, formalizing one widow's private devotion into a national center of Marian pilgrimage.

Kings of England themselves made the pilgrimage on foot in the centuries that followed, among them Henry III and Edward I. By the late Middle Ages, Walsingham stood alongside Canterbury as one of the two great pilgrimage destinations of the whole English Church.
Destroyed at the Reformation
Walsingham's centuries of continuous pilgrimage ended abruptly in 1538, when the priory was suppressed under Henry VIII's dissolution of the monasteries.
The venerated statue of Our Lady was carried to London and burned along with other images the reformers judged idolatrous.
This single, deliberate act silenced eight hundred years of English devotion at a stroke and left the shrine's very site nearly forgotten for more than three centuries.
A Restored Pilgrimage
Devotion to Our Lady of Walsingham was slowly revived in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, among both Catholics and Anglicans.
New shrines were built near the original site.

Pope Pius XI restored the ancient Slipper Chapel to Catholic use in 1934, and Walsingham has since regained its place as one of England's principal Marian pilgrimage destinations, drawing visitors from every Christian tradition in the country.

Pope Leo XIII had already granted a formal coronation to the restored image in 1897, and English bishops and popes since, including Benedict XVI and Francis, have continued to encourage devotion to Our Lady under this ancient title.
Legacy
Whatever the precise historical shape of Richeldis's own vision, it rests on a written account set down some four centuries after the events it describes.
The Church has long received it as a venerable and cherished tradition, one of the earliest Marian devotions in English Christian memory.
Across nearly a thousand years of interrupted and restored devotion, Our Lady of Walsingham remains a quiet reminder.
A shrine built out of one widow's private prayer can outlast even the empires and reformations that once tried to erase it.
